Um, as you're aware, we took this, item up at your last meeting. By way of background, Policy 865, which is currently on the books, is being recommended for deletion in its entirety and replacement with 6330, Distribution of Information and Posting of Schools on

School Grounds or during School-Sponsored Events. Uh, this policy, has, has been through many revisions beginning, several years ago before this board with F&O and then with this board but the previous LA&P Committee. It was heard once by the full board. It was sent back to this committee. You heard at your last meeting, and we are now here to take action. information that we received from individual citizens and from the advisory committees who chose to submit comments. We do have a presentation that just summarizes the comments. BoardDocs. Okay, so first we'll start with MSAC. If you can go to the next slide, please. MSAC began at, their first feedback was relative to lines six through eight in the section that reads, "Only requests from the following organization/entities to distribute and/or post materials within schools, on school grounds, or at school-sponsored activities may be approved upon the authorization of a principal or

LCPS building administrator." And I'm accentuating the word or, 'cause the feedback from MSAC was that it was ambiguous that the word or, whose decision takes precedence. Are approval split between two authorized parties? What if there is a principal and another building administrator, such as an assistant principal? So in consultation, with legal to remove that ambiguity, the following revision is recommended by the

administration for the committee to sent, to the end of the sentence on line eight, so it would read, "May be approved upon the authorization of the building principal or designee or the building administrator at non-school sites." And we believe that will clarify any ambiguity. Um, most of the time this would be a matter for a building principal, but we do have some centers where there is a, a,

a-- Or this building is a non-school site, and, the building administrator would have to make that determination. Any questions about that proposed change based upon the feedback from MSAC at line eight? Okay. The next comment from MSAC was at lines, forty-two to forty-three, the section of the policy that reads, "Advocate for or against a political campaign or political cause as further described in Section B2

below." And the comment from MSAC is that there's politics in everything, and anything can and likely will become a political cause. This term is vague. Um, I would, in response refer the committee down to lines seventy-three through seventy-nine, which provide three examples of political campaigns or political causes. As listed in the policy in those lines, number one, the election or defeat of any candidate; number two, the passage or defeat of any referendum

question; or number three, the passage or defeat of any matter pending before the school board, Loudoun County Board of Supervisors, the General Assembly, or Congress. Accordingly, administration is not recommending any further revisions to lines forty-two through forty-three since the policy does clarify what political cause or political campaign might mean in line seventy-three to seventy-nine. Any questions from the board members about,

lines forty-two through forty-three and the feedback from MSAC? Okay. The next, comment from MSAC was at lines forty-five and forty-six, the part of the policy that reads, "Are likely to cause substantial disruption of or a material interference with school activities." And I'm accentuating all of those words as

MSAC didThe comment being that the wording is subjective, particularly if the decision is being made by one person. The reasons and specifics for the denial should be documented so there's clear evidence showing the cause of the denial. In response, the administration would say we rely on our building principals and their professional judgment to determine what constitutes an event that is likely to cause substantial disruption or material interference with school activities. And accordingly, we are not recommending any further

revisions to lines forty-five and forty-six. Questions from the board members? Mr. Svenson. Yes. I just wanted to ask Mr. Allen if this language also tracks, y- legal precedent, Supreme Court language that... So it might be helpful if this is kind of a, a definition or term of art in the law. Thank you, Chair Svenson. Um, it, it is. It's arising out of Tinker versus Des Moines Independent Community School

District. Um, so th-that case out of the Supreme Court and its progeny, has expanded Tinker to provide that in de- det-determination of the likelihood of a material and substantial disruption is kind of a term of legal art, and schools may consider foreseeability of disruption. Um, and so this language is also in other policy, school board policies, in the student discipline suite.

Okay. All right. Then we'll, we'll move on. individual to be approached and does not allow for accountability if this section is not followed, and the recommendation from MSAC was that we add wording, something similar to, "A person may not be approached. Material may not be-- may only be distributed if the person approaches and requests such materials. fifty-six to sixty-four pertain to election days, which generally are non-school days, and the officials who are in charge of the polling would be responsible for generally anything that's occurring relative to the posting of political signs or, you know, they're-- wherever the polling place is, whether it's a school, a church, a community center, there, the rules apply as to what politicians can and cannot do with the electorate as they're approaching to,

to cast their vote. So accordingly, we're not recommending any changes to lines fifty-six to sixty-four since that section is pertinent to B1 election days, which generally are not school days. I just wanna hear- Okay. -everything that's in front of you. Yeah. by a member of the committee. It was not recommended by the administration that we include that section in the policy. three to be specific, three individuals who took the time to, follow the link and provide their, their own comment. September seventeenth is Constitution and Citizenship Day.

It's the time of year when most back-to-school nights occur and that this is an opportunity for civic engagement with parents at back-to-school nights about local election information, and it's an educational opportunity. So I, I would read that as they are in favor of section B3 as it was amended into the policy. To the contrary, another individual who identified themself as the LEAP representative for Eagle Ridge Middle School says, um-serving on the PTA board and helping at back to school nights,

I do not hesitate when I say the distribution of campaign materials at our back to school night borders on harassment if not crosses the line. Our community is diverse and many of our families do not know what or why they are being handed materials. They believe it is school related. They only-- they enter the event with confusion and frustration, which is a distraction to the purpose of back to school night. And they go on to make further comments, but I, I stopped, there, to signify their staunch,

support of removing B3 or not including that in the policy. And then the last, and third comment that we received, was from a student. And, as indicated on this slide, the student says that, "I strongly urge you to vote against this policy. As a student organizer of the Broad Run High School Against ICE walkout, the ability to distribute flyers was essential to our campaign. Restricting students' rights to protest, speak up, talk, pass

things amongst ourselves clearly violates our First Amendment rights. Students have voices and rights too, even within instructional time. While I understand not allowing posting of materials is not the business of the school, what is passed between students? We are also required to take U.S. government and political participation, and advocacy is taught to be a civic responsibility. Allow us to exercise our rights and display our interest in causes that are important to us." In response, the administration would point this

student and all students to Policy 8273, Student Speech and Expression, which was last revised in September of twenty twenty-four. And I'll read as indicated on the screen, "Students have the right to freedom of speech and expression during instructional and non-instructional time, both inside and outside classrooms or other areas where instruction is occurring. Such freedom of speech includes oral and written communication, student advocacy for social or political causes, and communications in different formats, such as

in publications, on clothing, or through electronic digital social media. This right does not extend to or include speech or other expressive conduct that violates Policy 8210, Introduction to Student Discipline, and/or that leads to or is likely to lead to substantial disruption or material interference with instructional time, school activities, or an invasion on the rights of others." So, in response to this comment, the administration's recommendation is that we would footnote into this policy, Policy

8273, Student Speech and Expression. That is all the feedback that we received, and I will pause here and turn it back over to the committee for further discussion about this policy.
